site.name: meadowos
site.summary: meadowos-clone Fictional self-hosted home OS "MeadowOS" marketing site (magazine / zine-style long-scroll narrative). Pages | File | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `index.html` | Single-page long scroll: thin top nav + progress bar; hero with hand-drawn SVG house and flower illustration; five chapters (Roman numerals I–V) of magazine-prose with pull quotes and chapter illustrations; mid-page "Garden" 6-card plant-app grid (Nextfile / Bramble / Cottage / Smithy / Hearth / Postcard); reviewer quotes; terminal-style .iso download block + platform pills + minimum / recommended specs; six numbered manifesto items; dark footer | | `styles.css` | Brand color #2F5233 dark green, accent terracotta + wheat yellow, cream paper background; Crimson Pro serif + Inter; cards with slight rotate + paper-shadow; responsive | | `script.js` | Top scroll progress bar; smooth anchor scrolling; clicking "Download .iso" triggers a fake download-progress modal (increments to 100% then shows SHA256 verification passed) |

run_plan.goal: Validate the MeadowOS single-page marketing journey end-to-end, with emphasis on story-to-garden-to-docs-to-download navigation, the fake ISO download experience, and mobile usability of the compact navigation controls.
run_plan.summary: The run should start at the top of the long-scroll landing page, confirm the anchored navigation/progress behavior, then work through the narrative sections and the Garden app grid to make sure the page’s key marketing content is reachable and readable. After that, the browser should validate the download section and the scripted download-progress modal, then check footer/community links and any recovery behavior for the placeholder external links. Because the prescan shows several small tap targets, the critical interactions should be repeated in a mobile viewport to verify touch usability and scrolling/anchor alignment.
assumptions: This site is a single-page experience only; no separate HTML pages were discovered in the prescan.
The visible '#'-style links and buttons are the primary interactive surface; external placeholders in the footer may not navigate anywhere meaningful.
The 'Get the .iso' button is expected to open a fake progress modal and not trigger a real file download.
The 'Story', 'Garden', and 'Docs' nav items are anchor links into sections on the same page, so validation should focus on scroll positioning and state changes rather than page loads.
risk_hotspots: Top navigation anchors: 'Story', 'Garden', 'Docs', and 'Get the .iso' are all small tap targets on mobile and may be hard to activate accurately.

Download CTA and scripted modal: the 'Download · meadowos-0.7.iso · 1.2 GB' button at the download section is the main conversion flow and should be checked for correct progress, completion, and verification messaging.
Footer links: 'GitHub' and 'Matrix room' are href='#' placeholders and need validation for non-breaking behavior and clear affordance.
Long-scroll anchor alignment: section jumps may land with headers hidden under the sticky top nav or progress bar.
Garden app cards: the 6-card feature grid is a major content block and may have hover/rotation or layout issues on smaller screens.

phases.title: Baseline landing and navigation
phases.objective: Establish the page structure, top-of-page state, and the behavior of the sticky navigation and progress indicator.
key_checks: Confirm the hero headline, subheading, and illustration render without truncation at the initial scroll position.
Click 'Story', 'Garden', and 'Docs' from the top nav and verify each anchor scrolls to the expected section.
Observe whether the top progress bar updates while scrolling through the page.
Check whether the sticky nav remains usable after a small scroll.
exit_criteria: All top-nav anchors have been exercised at least once.
The scroll/progress behavior has been observed in both idle and scrolled states.
No obvious layout breaks are seen in the hero or sticky header.

phases.title: Story section reading and anchor alignment
phases.objective: Validate the long-form narrative content and the page's readability/wayfinding through the story chapters.
key_checks: Scroll through chapters I–V and confirm headings, pull quotes, and chapter illustrations are legible in sequence.
Verify the 'Read time · ~6 min' cue stays contextually appropriate and does not overlap content.
Use the Story anchor to jump back into the section and check that the landing position is sensible.
Check for any awkward spacing or line-length issues in the magazine-style prose blocks.
exit_criteria: All story chapters have been viewed at least once.
At least one anchor jump into the story section has been validated.
No clipping/overlap issues are observed in the text-heavy sections.

phases.title: Garden feature grid validation
phases.objective: Exercise the featured app grid as the main adjacent product/storytelling flow and inspect the card layout behavior.
key_checks: Scroll to the Garden section and confirm all 6 app cards are visible: Nextfile, Bramble, Cottage, Smithy, Hearth, and Postcard.
Inspect card spacing, rotation, and paper-shadow styling for visual consistency.
Check whether the section remains readable and whether cards wrap cleanly on narrower viewports.
If any cards are interactive, confirm their click/tap behavior; if not, verify they are still presented as intended informational items.
exit_criteria: All six Garden cards are seen and identified.
No card-overlap or misalignment issues are present in desktop and mobile layouts.
The section is reachable via both scrolling and the Garden anchor.

phases.title: Docs and download conversion flow
phases.objective: Validate the documentation/download lead-in and the scripted ISO download experience from initiation to completion.
key_checks: Jump to the Docs section and verify the terminal-style .iso block, platform pills, and minimum/recommended specs are visible.
Activate the 'Download · meadowos-0.7.iso · 1.2 GB' button and confirm the fake download-progress modal appears.
Watch the modal increment to completion and confirm the final SHA256 verification passed state is shown.
Ensure the modal can be dismissed or otherwise does not trap the user after completion.
exit_criteria: The download CTA has been triggered successfully.
The progress modal reaches its terminal success state.
Return path from the modal is confirmed and the page remains functional afterward.

phases.title: Footer, placeholders, and recovery paths
phases.objective: Check secondary links and end-of-page affordances, especially placeholder external destinations and any fallback behavior.
key_checks: Scroll to the footer and verify the 'GitHub' and 'Matrix room' links are present and identifiable.
Activate each footer link and record whether it is a placeholder, inert, or produces any recovery behavior.
Confirm the footer styling remains legible in the dark theme and does not obscure link affordances.
If the page supports keyboard navigation, verify tab order reaches these links logically.
exit_criteria: Any placeholder behavior has been documented.
The end-of-page state does not introduce unexpected errors or broken UI.

phases.title: Mobile viewport validation
phases.objective: Repeat the most important interactions on mobile to verify touch targets, anchor usability, and long-scroll readability under constrained width.
key_checks: Re-check the header nav targets 'Story', 'Garden', 'Docs', and 'Get the .iso' for tap accuracy and accidental misfires.
Verify the page remains usable with the small tap targets flagged in the prescan.
Confirm the hero, Garden cards, and Docs/download section reflow cleanly without horizontal scrolling.
Repeat the download CTA and modal flow in mobile to ensure the scripted interaction still works.
exit_criteria: Critical anchor and CTA interactions have been repeated in mobile viewport.
No mobile-specific clipping, overlap, or unusable controls are observed beyond the already noted small-target risk.
The download flow and at least one anchor jump are confirmed on mobile.

coverage_targets.pages: Visit all known HTML pages discovered in the prescan; here that means fully covering index.html.
coverage_targets.features: Exercise the top navigation anchors, the long-scroll story content, the 6-card Garden grid, the Docs/specs block, the fake ISO download modal, and the footer links.
coverage_targets.mobile: Repeat the highest-value checks on mobile viewport: top nav taps, anchor jumps, the Garden section, and the download modal flow.

notes: Prioritize the scripted download flow because it is the only clearly stateful interaction in the prescan.
Since there is only one known page, breadth comes from sections and states rather than cross-page navigation.

prescan_summary.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
prescan_summary.visible_text_excerpt: MeadowOS Story Garden Docs Get the .iso Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. observation.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
observation.visible_text: MeadowOS Story Garden Docs Get the .iso Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or t

Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or t

observation.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
observation.visible_text: MeadowOS Story Garden Docs Get the .iso Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or t

observation.visible_text: MeadowOS Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or two or four people who would lik

observation.visible_text: MeadowOS Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or two or four people who would lik

observation.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
observation.visible_text: MeadowOS Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or two or four people who would lik
